lines.note: Hiban, ban ni arazu, means being off watch or not having one's turn; the negative Japanese matches não vigiar.

runs.text: caber ſua vez de vigiar. ¶ Item, O vigiar

lines.note: The gloss first says the watch is not one's turn, then introduces voluntarily watching nevertheless; this entire row is Portuguese.
Tōban contrasts the assigned watch with hiban; the rightmost abbreviated que continues the Portuguese definition below.

runs.text: cabe, ou pertence a alguem. Vt,

lines.note: The watch belongs to someone by turn; Fiban starts an example combining both statuses.
Hiban tōban naku tsumete iru means remaining on duty regardless of turn; the Portuguese always-watching explanation agrees.

runs.text: giando ſem ter deuer com lhe caber, ou não

lines.note: The watch continues whether or not the turn belongs to the watcher; retain deuer as the printed wording.
Caber sua vez closes the turn-taking condition; it is not a new capitalized Laber word.
Hibana is a fire-flower or spark/firework; Fi at the end begins the example continued below.
Hibana wo chiraite tatakō describes fierce fighting; chiraite is retained as printed rather than modernized to chirashite.

runs.text: Lugar de certas aruores como aci

lines.note: Hibara is a place of certain cypress-like trees; its initial i is faint but the headword is visible.
Prestes completes aciprestes across the physical break, finishing the tree comparison.
Hibari is the lark, glossed Calhandra; the headword's initial F was lost by OCR.
Hibarige is a horse coat resembling a lark's color; cavalo and cor clarify the two damaged Portuguese words.
Hibasami is the serpentine or match-holding part of a firearm, not an animal despite Serpe.
Hibashi are two long iron rods like small skewers; the pair is used as fire tongs.

runs.text: com que tomaõ o fogo, cu o atiçaõ.

lines.note: The rods take up or stir fire; preserve the printed conjunction and independent tilde positions rather than normalizing them.

Hibashita is an incomplete day or the portion lacking to make a whole day, as the Portuguese below states. Ichinichi is clear; the worn tararu is retained provisionally, although a negative tarazu would fit the gloss better. The surviving ink does not securely establish the missing internal letters.

runs.text: ou que lhe falta pera ſer inteiro.

lines.note: The day lacks something of being whole, supporting the incomplete-day interpretation of hibashita.
Hibi are cold-induced cracks; hibi ga kiruru is the example, and frio restores the final vowel of the gloss.

runs.text: Gretarem as maõs, pès, &c. com frio.

lines.note: Hands and feet crack from cold; Gretarem is the relevant Portuguese verb, not OCR Orearem.
Hibikase is causative resonance, 'make resound'; its inflection and the thunder example guide the damaged vowel reading.
Raiden ga kumo wo hibikasu means thunder makes clouds resound; the Japanese syntax and next gloss support the damaged n and a.

runs.text: O trouaõ faz retumbar as nuuens.

lines.note: The Portuguese repeats thunder making clouds reverberate, confirming the causative interpretation rather than an unrelated action.
Hibi ni means every day; it is distinct from the neighboring hibi cracks and hibiki resonance.
Hibiki is sound, but the entry also introduces a crack or break; both senses are kept rather than flattened into resonance alone.
Quebradura of a vessel or plank completes the second meaning; Fibiqi- begins its example below.
Hibiki ga iru, iku, ita gives the Japanese forms for a crack occurring; these forms were wrongly italicized as Portuguese in the draft.
The gloss says the crack or break exists or has formed, closing the example.
Hibiki, -u, iita is resounding; the printed ijta is retained rather than silently replacing its historical i/j appearance.
Toki wo dotto aguru koe is the raised battle cry; ma- starts makoto ni in the quotation.

runs.text: cotoni tenni fibiqi, ricugi xindô xite vo-

lines.note: Makoto ni ten ni hibiki, rikugi shindō shite describes sound echoing in heaven and shaking the earth; hibiki resolves OCR habiki.
Obitataxi completes the description of overwhelming sound; Tacax is the printed citation label, not automatically harmonized to another title.

runs.text: alarido que ſe aleuantou, verdadeiramẽte que

lines.note: The Portuguese identifies the raised shouting and clamour and introduces its truly thunderous effect.

runs.text: retumbando no ceo, & abalandoſe a terra era

lines.note: Echoing in heaven and shaking earth matches the quotation's ten and rikugi, strengthening the bilingual alignment.
Espantosa closes the description of an awe-inspiring or frightening event, not a separate headword.
Hibikiwatari means resound far and wide; retain the printed spacing in Retun bar pending finer typography review.
Mikata to teki no koe contrasts our side's and the enemy's voices in the long quotation.

runs.text: xifǒ ſanbiacu yorini fibiqi vatatte, tẽmo

lines.note: Shiho (four directions) and sanbyaku yori (more than three hundred ri) describe the battle cries carrying widely. The scan supports xifǒ, not xitǒ: f represents the historical h in 四方. Tẽmo begins the image of heaven falling, continued below; the exact abbreviated mark is retained.

runs.text: tachimachi vochi, cogicu mo vorete cata-

lines.note: Tachimachi vochi says “suddenly falling”; the following cogicu mo vorete describes the heavenly axes breaking, as the Portuguese exos do ceo confirms. The compound is worn, so cogicu remains provisional rather than being modernized or supplied with an unattested accent.
Katamuku ka to ayashiki hodo ni zo kikoyetari conveys seeming to hear the world tilt; the damaged muqucato is read as that sequence, with the printed q retained.
Taif is the source label; the scan supports book 15, not OCR 36. The translation begins the voices of both sides.

runs.text: dos inimigos ſoando por todas as partes, mais

lines.note: The enemies' voices sound on all sides, matching the quotation's directional language.

runs.text: de 300. legoas, parecia duuidarmos ſe as nu-

lines.note: The gloss gives more than 300 leagues and uncertainty whether the clouds were falling; this is literary scale, not a measured distance claim.

runs.text: uẽs cabião, & os exos do ceo quebrandoſe ſe

lines.note: The heavenly axes break and incline in the translation; retain the printed cabião rather than modernizing the falling-cloud wording.
The great estrondo explains the imagined collapse; the surviving strokes support inclinauão and estrondo over OCR garbling.

runs.text: Fibiraqi, u. l, fibiraqi itami, u.

lines.note: Hibiraki or hibiraki itami concerns stinging pain; the second form combines the same stem with itami rather than the OCR-separated fragments.
A wound burns or stings with pain; ferida and dor define the physical sensation.
Hibiǔ in kotoba no hibiǔ concerns a flaw in speech; the final marked u is faint, so this remains a useful human-review point rather than an assured lexical restoration.

runs.text: ro no falar. ¶ Item, Modo, ou geito do

lines.note: A second sense is manner or turn of speaking, extending beyond an outright error.

runs.text: falar, pollo qual ſe entende algũa couſa de que

lines.note: The manner of speaking allows an uncertain matter to be understood; falar and entende restore the coherent Portuguese clause.
Se duvida closes the doubtful matter inferred from speech; it is not a separate uncertainty annotation.
Hibiware, -uru, -eta is cracking open; the visible final r of abrir belongs to this row.
Boards exposed to sun are the example of cracking, giving physical context to hibiware.
Hibo means cords or straps for tying; the b is visible and matches the following compound.
A different hibo is a sorrowing mother, kanashimu hawa; the Portuguese mãy separates it from the cord sense.
Hibokashi is drying something, with algũa modifying the following cousa; the last a is present.
Ao fogo specifies drying by fire, completing the verb's definition.
Hibo otoshi or obi naoshi concerns a change in fastening dress; vobi, not ubi, is supported by the belt context.

runs.text: do de atar o cingidouro de tras como trazem

lines.note: The old mode ties the girdle behind, and the next row identifies the children using it.

runs.text: os mininos atè os noue annos, & cingirſe por

lines.note: The text specifies children up to nine years and a change to fastening in front; preserve that historical age statement.
Diante completes por diante, the front-fastening alternative.
Hibukure, -uru, -eta is blistering of the hand or another body part; uru restores the infinitive ending.

runs.text: parte do corpo queimada, ou eſcaldada.

lines.note: The blistered part was burned or scalded, explaining the fire-related compound.
Hibukure ga shita says a blister formed; the visible t corrects the OCR gap in xi.a.
Empo-la completes the blister caused by fire, not a separate noun entry.

runs.text: Cobertura de papel pera as lanter-

lines.note: Hibukuro is a paper covering for lanterns; papel pera restores the damaged material-and-purpose phrase.

runs.text: nas, ou que poem ſobre os candieiros.

lines.note: The covering is also put over lamps; poem is the printed verb, not porm.
Hibun is unreason or injustice; the Portuguese noun identifies the damaged letters without imposing a new sense.

runs.text: Reſplandor, ou rayo do ſol. Vt,

lines.note: Hikage here is sunlight or a ray, not shade yet; the Portuguese definition establishes the first sense.

runs.text: Entrar, ou dar o rayo do ſol

lines.note: Hikage sasu means sunlight falls or enters; the damaged letters are supported by both the headword and rayo do sol.
Hikage nodoka ni na- begins the sun becoming calm and clear; nodocani supplies the adverbial ni rather than OCR vi.
Nariyuku completes the gradual change; Feiq is a citation label preceding Lib. 4 and the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: o dia claro, & ſereno como no tempo da pri-

lines.note: The day becomes clear and serene like spring, translating nodoka ni nariyuku.

runs.text: ma vera. ¶ Item, Sombra contra os rayos

lines.note: Primavera completes before the second hikage sense, shade against sunlight; both meanings are explicitly present.
Hikage wo suru or koshirayuru means make shade; coxirayu- is the visible continuation stem, not cexirayu.

runs.text: Fazer ſombra, ou toldo pera ſe de fender

lines.note: Ru completes koshirayuru; a canopy is made to protect oneself, with the printed Portuguese spacing retained.
Do sol finishes the protection from sun, completing the shade sense.
Hikai, equated with tokoro, names bitter roots; Ficai is supported by the visible c and the botanical synonym.

runs.text: como cinouraſinhas amarelas que ſeruem de

lines.note: The roots resemble small yellow carrots and are medicinal; the comparison need not imply botanical identity.
Mezinha closes servem de mezinha, medicinal use of the roots.
Hikare, -uru, -eta is the passive of drawing or leading, as the Portuguese ser levado indicates.
Te wo hikaruru means being led by the hand; the object construction is preserved as printed.
Teki ni hikaruru means being taken by enemies, with ni marking the agent.
The enemy gloss ends before uma ni hikaruru, being carried or dragged by a horse.

runs.text: leuado do caualo deſenfreado, ou q̃ não obedece

lines.note: The horse is unbridled or disobedient; desenfreado is the adjective, not the OCR final e form.
Yoku ni hikaruru shifts to being led by desire, after the horse's bridle explanation.
Cubiҫa completes the figurative pull of greed or desire.
Hikari is light; hikari wo hanatsu is emitting light, with the complete hanatsu word visible.

runs.text: Dar, ou deitar de ſi claridade. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Giving off light completes the literal example; Item introduces a metaphorical extension.

runs.text: Per met. Reſplandecer, ou dar bom exemplo

lines.note: Per met. explains shining as giving a good example; exemplo is the relevant Portuguese noun.
A good deed completes the moral example; hikari wo tsutsu- begins concealing one's light.
Mu completes tsutsumu; concealing brightness can carry a figurative sense as explained below.

runs.text: ſe toma por encubrir as virtudes, nome,

lines.note: Concealing virtues or one's name explicates modest concealment, not loss of physical light alone.
The final &c. belongs to that explanation; the separate Fica- is already correctly recorded as catchword.
